children.name: Vital Signs from a Camera
children.blurb: Vital signs from a camera covers the estimation of pulse, breathing rate, and sometimes blood oxygen or blood pressure using ordinary video from a phone, laptop, or webcam rather than a contact sensor.

children.name: Wearable Data in Clinical Care
children.blurb: Wearable data in clinical care covers the continuous or near continuous physiological measurements collected by consumer and medical grade devices, including heart rate, heart rhythm, oxygen saturation, sleep stages, step counts, skin temperature and glucose levels.

children.name: Conversational Care and Its Limits
children.blurb: Conversational care covers the use of chat interfaces and voice agents to gather symptoms, offer initial guidance, and route patients to the right level of care.

children.name: Digital Signals of Mental Health
children.blurb: Digital signals of mental health cover the passive and active data that phones, wearables and keyboards produce which may relate to mood, sleep, activity and social contact.

sections.body: Telemedicine and triage is the part of medical AI that sits between a person and a clinician, deciding how urgent a problem is and what kind of care it needs. In practice this means chat interfaces that ask about symptoms and route people to emergency, urgent or routine care, phone cameras that estimate pulse and breathing from small color changes in the face, wearables that stream heart rate and sleep into clinical workflows, and conversational agents that offer support between appointments. The work is live rather than experimental: health systems use triage tools to sort incoming requests, and remote monitoring programs pull wearable data into dashboards that nurses review. Mental health is the newest edge, where typing patterns, voice and phone usage are studied as signals of mood or relapse.
sections.heading: What this covers

sections.body: Triage and routing are the most mature pieces, with several systems cleared for clinical use and others deployed quietly inside call centers, though accuracy drops on rare conditions and in patients who describe symptoms atypically. Camera vital signs work best in good light and steady position, and they are not a replacement for a cuff or a pulse oximeter. Wearables generate far more data than most clinics can absorb, and the evidence that continuous monitoring changes outcomes is uneven across conditions. Conversational care has real limits: it can hold a structured interview but struggles with ambiguity, and it should not be the only thing standing between a person and urgent help. Mental health signals are the least settled area, with small studies, unclear consent practices and a real risk of false alarms. This site tracks 1,000 medical AI models and 6 active product liability and wrongful death lawsuits against AI companies, which is a reminder that errors in this section are not abstract.
sections.heading: Where the work stands

sections.body: Start with Symptom Triage and Routing for the front door of the field, the logic that decides who needs care now and who can wait. Vital Signs from a Camera covers the contactless measurement layer, useful when a sensor is unavailable or a patient cannot be touched. Wearable Data in Clinical Care follows the stream after it leaves the wrist, and deals with the practical problem of turning continuous readings into something a clinician can act on. Conversational Care and Its Limits is the honest counterweight, describing what dialogue systems can and cannot do and where a human must take over. Digital Signals of Mental Health closes the section on the most speculative ground, where behavioral data is read as a psychiatric signal and the ethical questions are still open. Read together, these pages move from routing to measurement to monitoring to conversation to inference, which is also the order in which the evidence gets thinner.
